synopsis: FMVSS 127 was finalized on 9 May 2024 and requires AEB on new US light vehicles by 1 September 2029; its scope ends at 4,536 kg GVWR, so it is an on-road reference rather than a rule applicable to off-road machines [f1513, f2831]. It requires lead-vehicle avoidance up to 62 mph, forward-collision warning, and pedestrian AEB at 10–73 km/h in daylight and darkness; specified false-activation tests fail when peak deceleration exceeds manual braking by at least 0.25 g, while the braking algorithm remains the manufacturer's choice [f15420, f11691, f15421, f15422, f6185]. The timetable remains contested: manufacturers challenged the rule over false-activation risk, and in March 2026 the Department of Transportation proposed preparing a two-year lead-time extension, which the booklet explicitly says was not adopted [f1228, f2537]. Unnecessary braking is the dominant documented on-road AEB failure mode, but investigation outcomes require care: Tesla's probe closed on 29 June 2026 with 695,000 vehicles and about 25,900 incident reports yet no crashes, injuries or defect finding, while the Detroit Assurance investigation escalated in October 2025 and reproduced braking on a steel trench plate [f115, f11170, f11171, f1317, f1812]. For heavy-machine validation, the corpus points to necessary adaptations for stopping distance and equipment, alongside NHTSA heavy-vehicle stationary-target false-positive tests and a −0.05 g braking-onset threshold [f1732, f6192, f6193]. Other evidence highlights both benefits and safety-management failures: IIHS reported a 78% reduction in backing-crash involvement with rear automatic braking, camera and sensors, while NTSB's Uber fatality investigation found disabled factory emergency braking, a one-second action suppression despite emergency recognition 1.2 seconds before impact, and deficient safety risk management and culture [f15436, f15432, f15433, f15434].
